AI for Mobility · CGN 6933 · Module 2 companion

How DETR detects: 100 learned questions, one answer per vehicle

A camera at an intersection sees an unknown number of road users. A detector has to hand back a set: one box per car, truck, pedestrian and bicycle, no more and no fewer. DETR (Carion et al., 2020) reaches that set without the delete-the-duplicates step every earlier detector needed. This page runs the original DETR on eight real traffic photographs, puts a same-sized Faster R-CNN next to it, trains a small DETR from scratch on a synthetic drone view of a road, and then follows the idea into lane maps, tracking and 3-D perception for automated vehicles. Every number on the page comes from a run you can repeat.

The problem DETR solves

Counting turning movements, measuring a queue, checking a crosswalk for pedestrians: each one starts by turning a frame into a list of objects. The list has no fixed length, and nothing in the frame says which pixels belong to which vehicle. Before 2020, detectors handled this by proposing far too many boxes and deleting the overlapping ones with a hand-written rule, non-maximum suppression (NMS). DETR asks a fixed number of learned questions instead, and is trained so that each object is claimed by exactly one question.

What you already know that carries straight over

  • From Sept 3 (CNNs): the backbone. DETR's ResNet-50 has weights, exactly as many as the Faster R-CNN on this page. The two detectors differ only in what sits on top.
  • From last week (BERT): the encoder. It is self-attention over tokens. Here a token is one cell of the ResNet feature map, which covers a 32 × 32-pixel square of the resized frame.
  • From Sept 24 (cross-attention): the decoder. A small set of query vectors reads the image tokens, the same way a text query read the dashcam frames in the multimodal crash-warning example.
  • From transportation planning: the training trick. Deciding which question owns which vehicle is the assignment problem, the unit-supply case of the transportation problem. A vehicle tracker solves the same problem every frame when it links new detections to existing tracks.

The data. Eight openly licensed photographs from Wikimedia Commons: a signalised intersection in Jacksonville (dashcam), I-35 in Austin from an overpass, I-95 in Miami at rush hour, trucks on the I-5 Interstate Bridge, cyclists at a pop-up protected intersection, a work-zone ramp on I-10 in Tallahassee, the Shirley Highway at dusk in the early 1970s, and a shopping-centre parking lot from the air. Authors and licences are listed at the bottom of every tab. Tab 6 also uses of the FL511 Tampa Bay camera frames from Lab 6. The models are DETR-R50 with the paper's own weights and torchvision's Faster R-CNN R50-FPN (COCO). Both are trained on the 80 COCO categories, so "car", "truck", "bus", "person" and "bicycle" are what they can name. Tab 5's road is synthetic, drawn by a short generator in the training script.

1 · The model: a CNN, a BERT-style encoder, and 100 questions

DETR has four parts. A ResNet-50 turns the frame into a grid of feature vectors. A transformer encoder lets every grid cell look at every other. A transformer decoder lets 100 learned object queries read that grid. Two small heads turn each query into a class and a box. Pick a frame to see the real shapes.

The key equation

ŷᵢ = ( softmax(Wcls hᵢ) , σ(MLP(hᵢ)) ), i = 1 … 100 h₁…₁₀₀ = Decoder( q₁…₁₀₀ ; Encoder( proj(ResNet(x)) + pos ) )
xthe frame, resized so its short side is 800 px
ResNet(x)a grid of 2,048-number feature vectors, one per 32 × 32-pixel square
proj, posa 1 × 1 convolution down to 256 numbers per cell, plus a fixed 2-D sine code that says where the cell is (row, column)
qᵢobject query i: a learned 256-number vector. There are exactly 100 of them, the same 100 for every frame.
hᵢwhat query i has gathered after 6 decoder layers
Wclsa linear layer to scores: 91 COCO class ids plus one extra, ∅ = "no object"
σ(MLP)a 3-layer network ending in a sigmoid: the box as (centre x, centre y, width, height), each a fraction of the frame

In words: each of 100 learned questions reads the encoded frame and answers with a class (which may be "nothing") and a box. The answers are produced in parallel, all 100 at once. Nothing is generated word by word as in a GPT, and nothing is deleted afterwards.

Where the parameters are

The two detectors have nearly the same size: weights for DETR and for Faster R-CNN. Both carry the same -weight ResNet-50. What differs is the head. Faster R-CNN spends its head weights on a feature pyramid, a region-proposal network and a box classifier. DETR spends on six encoder and six decoder layers.

The 100 object queries are the smallest line in the table: numbers (100 × 256). They are the reason the model can hand back at most 100 objects, whatever the frame holds. Tab 6 measures what that means for a parking lot.

How many tokens does a frame become?

The grid is ⌈H/32⌉ × ⌈W/32⌉. The encoder compares every token with every token, so its attention table grows with the square of the token count. The decoder compares 100 queries with every token, so it grows linearly. Check the calculator against the measured frames: the Jacksonville frame (1,920 × 1,080) is resized to and becomes a grid = tokens.

Going deeper: why queries start empty and keep their position

In the decoder each query has two parts. The content starts as a vector of zeros and is rewritten by every layer. The query position qᵢ is the learned vector, and it is added again before every attention call, the same way the image's sine code is added to the keys. Because the content starts empty, all a query can bring to layer 1 is its learned position. That is why each query ends up specialising in a region and box size of the frame (tab 6 measures it on FL511 frames). Later DETR variants (Conditional DETR, DAB-DETR) make this explicit by turning the query position into a reference point or an anchor box. Source: Carion et al., End-to-End Object Detection with Transformers, ECCV 2020, §3.2 and Fig. 7.

2 · 100 questions, a handful of answers

Every frame gets exactly 100 answers. Most are "no object". Below, the top strip is DETR's answer sheet for the selected frame, one bar per query. Slide the threshold, then switch to Faster R-CNN to see what an NMS-based detector produces before it cleans up.

Read the strip. Each bar is one query, numbered 0 to 99. Its height is the probability the query gives to its most likely class, and its colour shows the class. The grey part is its probability of "no object". On the Jacksonville frame queries are more than 90% sure there is nothing for them. In the parking lot only is: almost every question is busy.
One vehicle, two answers. DETR's suppression works per object, not per label. A pickup or a large SUV is sometimes claimed twice, as "car" and as "truck", because the line between those two COCO classes is blurry for them. At the last decoder layer the Jacksonville frame still has overlapping pairs across classes, against within a class. Class-wise NMS would not remove them either.
Before you trust this comparison
Baseline
Faster R-CNN with the same ResNet-50 and nearly the same parameter count, the same 800-px resize, and the course's canonical pipeline: suppression off inside the model, score filter, then class-wise NMS at IoU 0.5.
Split

3 · Training: match first, then grade

To grade 100 answers against, say, 12 labelled vehicles, you first have to decide which answer is supposed to be which vehicle. DETR makes that decision fresh for every training image, with the cheapest one-to-one assignment. The 12 matched queries are graded on class and box. The other 88 are told "∅, no object". A second query on the same car is graded as wrong. That is what teaches the model not to produce duplicates.

The key equations

σ̂ = argminσ Σᵢ C( yᵢ , ŷσ(i) ) C = − p̂(cᵢ) + 5·‖bᵢ − b̂‖₁ + 2·(1 − GIoU(bᵢ, b̂)) L = Σᵢ [ − log p̂σ̂(i)(cᵢ) + 5·‖bᵢ − b̂σ̂(i)‖₁ + 2·(1 − GIoU) ] + 0.1 · Σunmatched − log p̂(∅)
yᵢ = (cᵢ, bᵢ)labelled object i: its class and its box (centre, width, height as fractions of the frame)
σan assignment: which query answers for which label, at most one each
Cthe cost of pairing a label with a query: low if the query already says the right class and draws a close box
5, 2the paper's weights on box distance (L1) and box overlap (generalised IoU)
0.1down-weight on the ∅ lessons, because most queries are unmatched in every image

In words: find the cheapest one-to-one pairing of labels and answers, then grade each pair, and grade every unpaired answer as "should have said nothing".

Try it on a real frame

The "labels" here are stand-ins: Faster R-CNN's confident boxes for road users (cars, trucks, buses, motorcycles, people and bicycles at score ≥ 0.7, after NMS), playing the part of an annotator. White dashed boxes are the labels, coloured boxes the queries graded as them, and the white lines join each pair. The predictions are DETR's real answers from the decoder layer you choose. Layer 1 is the rough first draft, layer 6 the final answer.

Does the matching rule matter? Three ways to train the same small DETR

The mini-DETR of tab 5 was trained three times on the same synthetic road scenes, with the same seed, steps each. Only the rule that decides which query answers for which vehicle changed:

  • Hungarian: DETR's one-to-one matching.
  • Ordered list: vehicles are sorted by lane and then by position, and handed to queries 0, 1, 2… in that order. A list instead of a set.
  • Top-3, one-to-many: each vehicle is the target of its three cheapest queries. This is the style of label assignment used by YOLO-type detectors, and it gives a richer training signal.

Crowd test: recall with more vehicles than training ever showed (training scenes had 0 to 12)

Going deeper: why GIoU and L1 together, and why 0.1 on ∅

L1 distance on (centre, width, height) treats a 4-pixel error on a distant car the same as on a bus in the foreground, although it is a much bigger mistake for the small one. Generalised IoU (Rezatofighi et al., 2019) is scale-invariant and still gives a useful gradient when two boxes do not overlap at all, which is where plain IoU is flat at zero. Using both keeps the absolute and the relative error in view. The ∅ weight matters because in a typical training image 90 or more of the 100 queries are unmatched. At full weight those easy "nothing here" lessons swamp the few real ones. DETR divides them by 10. DETR also applies this whole loss after every decoder layer (auxiliary losses), so layer 1 is trained to produce a usable draft. That is what lets tab 4 read the drafts layer by layer. Source: Carion et al. 2020, §3.1 and §4.

4 · Inside the decoder: how DETR does NMS without NMS

In each decoder layer the queries attend to each other before they look at the image. A query can therefore see that another query is already claiming a vehicle and back off. Read the six layers' drafts and watch duplicates disappear.

Where does each answer look?

Click a box. The heat map is that query's cross-attention in the last decoder layer, averaged over the 8 heads: how much of its reading it spent on each 32 × 32 cell. Switch to the encoder view to see the self-attention from the cell at the box's centre.

What to notice. Across all eight frames, confident vehicles touch less than 1% of the token cells (median ). Their queries still put a median of their last-layer cross-attention on those few cells: the decoder reads the object, not the scene. The paper's observation is that the last decoder layer concentrates on extremities (wheels, bumpers, roof edges): the encoder has already grouped pixels into instances, so the decoder only needs the boundaries.

This is the whole DETR recipe at a size that trains on a laptop CPU: a 4-layer CNN, 2 encoder layers, 3 decoder layers, object queries, weights. It was trained from scratch for steps on synthetic top-down scenes of a four-lane road, with Hungarian matching. The trained model runs in your browser. Drag a vehicle to move it. Double-click a vehicle to remove it. Hover a query below to see where it reads the road (its cross-attention in the last decoder layer). What each query learned to ask

The queries were never told what to specialise in. Below are the box centres each query predicts across fresh test scenes, one colour per query, counting only answers with p(object) > 0.5. Hover a query above to isolate it.

More vehicles than questions

The capacity is per zone, not per frame. Because each query owns a stretch of one lane, a queue overloads the few queries that cover it long before the road holds 16 vehicles. Eight cars queued in a single lane were found at recall ( test scenes). The same number of cars spread two per lane were found at . Part of the gap is that the random training scenes almost never packed one lane this tightly, which is itself the lesson: a detector for queue lengths at a stop bar has to be trained on queues. Press "Queue 8 cars in one lane" above to watch it happen.
The road scenes are synthetic. Generator, training script and checkpoints: mini_detr.py.

6 · Where it breaks

Three limits matter for transportation work: a hard ceiling on how many objects one frame can hold, weakness on small objects, and training cost. Each one is measured here on the same images and models.

The 100-question ceiling

The controlled test tiles the Jacksonville frame 1, 4, 9 and 16 times. Every tile is the same picture at the same scale, so the only thing that changes is how many objects the frame holds.

Vehicles = car, truck, bus or motorcycle at score ≥ 0.5 (Faster R-CNN after NMS). "Sure of ∅" = queries giving more than 90% to "no object". The natural scenes are processed at the standard 800-px resize. Both detectors' counts are what they said, not ground truth. The point is the gap between them and the share of DETR's questions left free.

Small objects

Each question has a favourite place: 100 queries on FL511 cameras

Every query answers on every frame, so its boxes can be collected. Below are the box centres of one query over Tampa Bay FL511 frames from Lab 6, with no score threshold, as in Fig. 7 of the paper. Pick a query.

A query that answers anywhere would scatter its centres across the frame, with a typical distance from their mean of frame widths. The median query's spread is . Queries that never named an object at p > 0.5 on any of these frames: . The average FL511 frame got confident answers. The frames are the 224 × 224 images packaged for Lab 6, enlarged to 480 × 480, so small vehicles are softer than in the original feeds.

Compute

On this page's CPU benchmark (2 threads, a input), DETR spends of its time in the ResNet-50 backbone, so the transformer is not where the cost is. Training is where the cost is: the paper trains for 500 epochs on COCO (300 for the baseline, about 3 days on 16 V100 GPUs), many times the schedule a Faster R-CNN needs. Deformable DETR reports better accuracy, especially on small objects, with 10 times fewer training epochs.

Before you trust these limits
Baseline
Faster R-CNN R50-FPN with the same backbone, run at the same resize. In the tiling test, also with its proposal budget raised to match the picture (a setting you can change without retraining).
Split
No labels on these photographs, so the counts are detections, not accuracy. The COCO numbers quoted are the paper's, on its validation set.
Ugly cases
The ceiling is a property of the trained weights. Adding queries means retraining. Tiling a large frame into crops and detecting each crop is the usual workaround, at the cost of objects cut by tile edges.

7 · Queries beyond boxes

The lasting idea in DETR is not the box. It is a fixed set of learned queries, trained with a set-matching loss, that each claim one thing. Change what a query answers and you get a different tool. Each card below names the paper, the transportation task, the data it needs and the classical method it competes with.

The same game on your own data

Ask the three questions from the transformer-architecture companion. What is a token? What may attend to what? What does position mean? Then add a fourth: what is one answer? Three set-prediction framings of traffic problems to try. Treat them as proposals, not results, and check the literature before you build one:

  • Congestion episodes on a time–space diagram. Tokens are detector-station × 5-minute cells of a speed heatmap. Each query answers with one episode: onset time, clearance time, upstream and downstream milepost, and a class (recurring, incident, work zone). Matching handles the fact that a day has 0 to 10 episodes. The classical baseline is a speed threshold plus connected components on the same heatmap.
  • Platoons in trajectory data. Tokens are vehicles in a NGSIM or highD snapshot. Each query answers with one platoon: a leader, a member list and a headway class. The baseline is a time-headway rule (for example, gaps under 2 s).
  • Incidents from a 511 event feed plus detectors. Tokens are detector readings and free-text reports. Each query answers with one incident and its location. The baseline is the California algorithm plus operator reports.
The catch is labels. A set loss needs a labelled set for every training example. COCO's labels cover about 1.5 million object instances, all drawn by hand. For episodes or platoons, labels have to come from a rule, a simulator, or an agency's event log, and the model can only become as good as those labels are.

When to reach for it

Applications

Before you trust a DETR result
Baseline
A detector of the same backbone and size trained the classical way (Faster R-CNN, or a YOLO-family model with NMS), plus the non-learning method the agency uses today (a loop count, a manual count of a video sample).
Split
By camera and by time of day, never by random frame: neighbouring frames of one video are nearly identical, and a random split leaks them into the test set (Lab 6 split by camera for this reason).
Ugly cases
Frames with more objects than queries; vehicles under 40 px tall; night; occluded queues, where both DETR's learned suppression and an IoU threshold are guessing; vehicles the label set calls by two names (pickup, SUV, van).

Check yourself

  1. A county wants to count occupied spaces in a 600-space park-and-ride from a single drone photograph. A vendor offers a DETR-based counter. What would you ask before buying, and what would you change in the setup to stay under the query ceiling?
  2. Your intersection camera feeds a tracker that computes turning movements. Duplicates and missed vehicles hurt the counts in different ways. Which detector behaviour in tabs 2 and 4 worries you more for a protected left-turn bay with a 10-vehicle queue, and how would you test it with 2 hours of video?
  3. A colleague says "DETR has no NMS, so its counts are always cleaner." Using the cross-class duplicates and the dense-queue result, write the two sentences you would reply with.
  4. You have 400 labelled frames of a new class, a downed traffic signal head after a hurricane. Would you fine-tune DETR, fine-tune a YOLO-family model, or try an open-vocabulary detector first? Name the data and the baseline you would use to decide.
